comparator.name: Law
comparator.sourceNotes: Current September-2026 programme tables and adopted 2026–2027 TLS programme-specific Appendix 1d Articles 30–35 confirm the Dutch-taught general Law LLB, sixty credits in each of the first two years and forty-two required third-year credits plus an eighteen-credit minor. The 8-EC thesis, 90-EC entry thresholds and non-credit Skills Lab prerequisite are explicit. The standard minor pathway is retained. The optional exchange alternative requires Examination Board approval under Article 35 and is not combined with this pathway. General legal research in the dated thesis entry controls over the recruitment page’s stray company-law topic wording. No Corporate Law route is selected for this generic target.
components: The general Law LLB is taught in Dutch, with individual English-language courses. The non-credit Dutch language test and student-development activities are retained outside the 180-EC total.
Introduction to Criminal Law and Criminal Procedure
This introduction builds on first-year constitutional law. The course is completed after the autumn constitutional introduction.
Second-year property, contract, liability and criminal courses deepen the respective first-year foundations. Completing all first-year courses supplies those foundations.
The dedicated procedure course builds on Introduction to Criminal and Criminal Procedure Law and Procedural-Law Practical Skills from Year 1.
The dated Legal Philosophy B course examines the EU as a legal and political union, including representation, legitimacy, direct effect and supremacy.

Entry requires at least 90 EC at registration; credits obtained after registration do not satisfy that threshold. The course includes mandatory attendance, legal-source research, written procedural documents, pleading training and an oral moot court. This pathway completes both earlier years before registration.

The 8-EC thesis begins in the autumn and spans the academic year. At least 90 EC must be earned when teaching begins. For students who started in September 2025 or later, a completed Tilburg Skills Lab is also required. Both earlier years and the non-credit Skills Lab are completed before Year 3. The thesis develops an independent legal research question, framework, proposal and paper; no particular legal topic is assumed.

Eighteen EC remain for an approved minor: Law in Practice, Law and a Sustainable Future, an outside minor or an approved custom package. No particular minor is imposed. The optional exchange requires separate approval and substitution under the regulations; it is not added to this 180-EC minor pathway.

courses: Business & Economy in the Age of AI
New Issues in Contemporary Social Theory

core: Law in social context, legal reasoning, interpretation and the purposes of legal rules
Private, civil, property and contract law
Criminal law, liability and criminal procedure
European Union, international and comparative legal systems
Legal practice, research, advocacy, decision-writing and responsible use of AI
Legal history, company and tax law, and philosophy of law
questions: How should law respond to sustainability problems and the use of artificial intelligence in legal research?
How do legal reasoning, advocacy and institutional design support professional and public-sector legal work?

trace: develops scholarly reading, research questions, academic writing, reflection and civic collaboration as the common foundation
examines AI’s economic and institutional implications, regulation, corporate responsibility, labour and inequality through business cases and country research
examines legal frameworks for cross-border contracts, trade, finance, intellectual property and digital commerce, with advisory assignments and simulated arbitration
introduces economic choice, markets, strategic interaction and government’s economic role as specific foundations for analysing regulation
examines incentives, uncertainty, strategic behaviour, labour/capital markets and externalities as an economic complement to legal regulation
examines public goods, taxation, spending, externalities and redistribution through policy models and research; this is an economic contribution rather than tax-law doctrine
examines trade, institutions, policy conflict and cross-border business decisions, supporting the international commercial context of legal practice
develops business models and the functions of enterprises, providing organisational context and the formal foundation for transnational business law without claiming company-law doctrine
develops empirical design, measurement, statistics and a data-collection project as a methodological complement to socio-legal inquiry
examines motivation, leadership, teams, power, conflict and organisational change, including evidence synthesis for organisational cases
develops bargaining, interests, power, trust and strategic conflict management through negotiation simulations and scenario design
examines institutions, power, participation, justice and collective decisions in sustainability, with stakeholder consultation and policy advice/evaluation
introduces planetary boundaries and scientific methods for understanding environmental pressures and sustainability interventions
examines climate science, impacts, adaptation, mitigation, justice and governance, supplying scientific and social substance for environmental regulation
introduces legal traditions, public/private law, justice and social context through case briefs, legal interpretation, mock trials and a socio-legal proposal
examines human-rights law, protection institutions, landmark cases and philosophical justifications through legal and normative argument
examines criminal liability, punishment, criminalisation, excuses, offences and participation, with legal-advice memoranda and a criminology research proposal
examines international legal sources, state responsibility, institutions, force, human rights and treaty politics through legal cases and critical research
compares constitutional structures, rights, courts and judicial review, with administrative participation, remedies and procedural fairness
examines property, tort and contract rights across legal systems through legal briefs, comparative contract research and simulated mediation
examines EU institutions, competences, legal effect, remedies, citizenship and free movement through current judgments and legal cases
develops ethical interpretation, normative argument and independent positions on moral theory and practical questions relevant to legal judgement
examines political authority, rights, human nature and social order through primary texts and normative argument
examines democracy, institutions, elections and political actors through empirical comparison, giving concrete political context to constitutional law
examines international relations, conflict and cooperation through theories, cases and a UN simulation, complementing international legal institutions
examines EU integration, representation, legitimacy and policymaking, including empirical parliamentary research that complements EU legal analysis
examines policy-making processes and alternative analytical frameworks through a sugar-policy case and policy memos, supporting the legal-governance perspective
examines conflict, humanitarian law, human rights, peacebuilding and transitional justice through interdisciplinary research and a policy brief
examines social institutions, inequality, identity and boundaries through social theory and evidence, complementing analysis of law’s social context
develops qualitative design, interviews, documentary inquiry, coding and interpretation for empirical investigation of social and institutional questions
examines environmental-justice movements, collective action and feminist/anticolonial perspectives through actual environmental cases
examines civil society, trust, public spheres, solidarity and social repair through theory and empirical study of an organisation or movement
develops rhetorical analysis, argument construction, debating and public speaking; its communication contribution is distinguished from legal procedure
examines climate communication, public argument and contested policy through media analysis and an intervention in public debate
examines persuasion, framing and ethics through research and community projects, complementing professional communication rather than supplying courtroom training
examines representations of ecological risk, scientific knowledge and human–environment relations as forces in public debate and environmental ethics

alternatives.label: Law, society & legal institutions
alternatives.labelReason: Study law through comparative constitutional, private, criminal, human-rights, European, international and transnational business law. Political institutions, social theory, economics, ethics and empirical research support analysis of how legal rules operate in society.
alternatives.concept: Study law through comparative constitutional, private, criminal, human-rights, European, international and transnational business law. Political institutions, social theory, economics, ethics and empirical research support analysis of how legal rules operate in society.
progression: Verified all assigned offerings and earlier formal prerequisites. The law gateway precedes dependent law courses, business foundations precede transnational business law, and research statistics precedes dependent economics and negotiation. Introductory political and sociological study precedes advanced EU/civil-society analysis where selected.

alternatives.label: Law, sustainability & governance
alternatives.labelReason: Study law and sustainability through the UCR law sequence, transnational business law and public governance. Climate science, sustainability, public economics, policy analysis, environmental justice and communication provide specific perspectives on regulatory and collective-action problems.
alternatives.concept: Study law and sustainability through the UCR law sequence, transnational business law and public governance. Climate science, sustainability, public economics, policy analysis, environmental justice and communication provide specific perspectives on regulatory and collective-action problems.
progression: Verified every assigned offering and earlier formal prerequisite. Law and business foundations precede dependent law courses, statistics precedes Public Economics, and sustainability foundations precede Governance of Sustainability. This option does not assume a partner project or a specialised environmental-law course at UCR.
alternatives.distinctness: This option combines the legal core with sustainability foundations, climate, environmental governance, public policy, environmental justice and environmental communication. The closest option gives more space to political thought, comparative politics, international relations, qualitative inquiry and negotiation.

alternatives.label: Legal practice, advocacy & organisations
alternatives.labelReason: Study legal practice through private, criminal, constitutional, European, international and transnational business law. Negotiation, rhetorical argument, organisational behaviour, AI governance and empirical research support legal problem-solving and collaboration.
alternatives.concept: Study legal practice through private, criminal, constitutional, European, international and transnational business law. Negotiation, rhetorical argument, organisational behaviour, AI governance and empirical research support legal problem-solving and collaboration.
progression: Verified all assigned offerings and earlier formal prerequisites. The law gateway precedes dependent law courses, business foundations precede transnational business law, and research statistics precedes dependent economics and negotiation. Introductory political and sociological study precedes advanced EU/civil-society analysis where selected.
alternatives.distinctness: This option retains the legal core while giving more space to international business, organisational psychology, AI governance, rhetoric and applied persuasion. The closest option instead places more weight on political philosophy, comparative politics, EU political institutions, peace/conflict and civil-society theory; the sustainability option concentrates on environmental governance.

selection.assessment: Retained three sequentially justified concepts: a broad law-and-society response, the evidenced sustainability/legal-governance priority and the evidenced practice/advocacy priority. Each retains substantial legal study and makes distinct choices in complementary disciplines. All pairs meet at least thirty EC each way and have distinct organising purposes. Production stops at the maximum of three; the options are not claimed to reproduce Tilburg’s minors or specialist Dutch procedural training.

blocks: Both examine technology, economic change, institutions and regulation in society. UCR concentrates on AI, firms and economic governance; Tilburg integrates technological, law-and-economics and legal-psychological perspectives.

Both develop legal-source analysis, reasoned written legal advice and oral advocacy in a simulated dispute. UCR uses transnational business arbitration; Tilburg uses Dutch judicial pleadings and procedural documents.

Both address methods of resolving disputes. UCR develops negotiation and bargaining through simulations; Tilburg also provides Dutch civil procedure, hearings and fact-finding. The relationship concerns the dispute-resolution part only.
Both develop legal concepts, legal-source interpretation, reasoning and case analysis, while situating law in a wider social and normative context.

Both examine fundamental rights, their legal and philosophical foundations, and national/international protection. Tilburg additionally concentrates on their operation in the Dutch and EU legal orders.
Both examine legality, causation, intent, guilt, justifications, excuses, attempts and participation as grounds and limits of criminal liability.

Both provide substantive public-international-law study. UCR combines foundational sources and institutions with contemporary legal cases and critical perspectives; the relationship is partial rather than a claim of identical specialist coverage.
Both examine state organisation, legislation, government institutions, rights and constitutional constraints. UCR adopts a comparative approach rather than a dedicated Dutch sequence.
Both examine property, tort and contract concepts, rights and obligations through legal cases. UCR compares multiple legal systems; Tilburg establishes Dutch private-law foundations.
Both examine the EU legal order, effects on national law, citizenship, free movement and legal protection. Tilburg also addresses competition law and procurement.

Both develop normative analysis of moral and social problems. UCR provides ethical theories and argument; Tilburg integrates these questions specifically with positive law and political/legal institutions.

Both examine the EU as a political and institutional union, representation and legitimacy. Tilburg frames these as questions of legal/political philosophy; UCR combines institutional analysis with empirical political research.
No selected course centres European legal history; general historical or political context is not substituted for legal-historical study.
Criminal Law and Criminal Justice has its strongest primary placement with advanced criminal liability. No second course is counted for this combined introductory substantive/procedural course.
Business foundations and transnational commercial law provide context, but no selected course centres Dutch corporation/partnership formation, organisation and termination.
The selected international and EU law courses have stronger primary placements with the dedicated second-year courses and are not counted again.
Comparative Constitutional Law includes administrative principles but is placed with constitutional law; no additional course supplies the dedicated Dutch administrative-law introduction.
Legal and communication skills occur across the UCR options, but no additional course provides the dedicated procedural-document training across criminal, private and administrative law.
Public Economics supplies a complementary analysis of taxation and redistribution, not the substantive Dutch tax-law rules of this course.
Principles of Private Law is placed with the broad private-law introduction; no second course supplies the dedicated Dutch property-law deepening.

Contract content is developed within selected private and business law courses, but their strongest primary placements are the private-law introduction and simulated legal-dispute practice. No course is counted twice.
The selected constitutional/administrative and human-rights courses support parts of the subject, but no separate course develops this dedicated Dutch judicial-protection sequence.
Private Law includes tort and liability but is already placed with the broader introductory course; no second course is counted for dedicated Dutch tort-law study.
Substantive criminal liability and a legal-aid simulation do not reproduce the dedicated Dutch criminal-process sequence.
Comparative methods occur within the UCR legal courses, but no additional course provides this dedicated global legal-traditions sequence.
Economic and organisational courses offer complementary perspectives on work and institutions, but no selected course provides Dutch individual/collective labour-law doctrine.
No compulsory Dutch legal thesis is scheduled at UCR. Optional independent research appears separately outside scheduled credits.
Open minor space remains unspecified; no particular minor or exchange package is invented.

notes.text: Tilburg Law provides a sustained Dutch doctrinal and procedural sequence, legal-practice training and a required legal thesis. UCR combines substantial comparative and international legal study with related disciplines. The partial relationships do not reproduce Tilburg’s specialist Dutch-law coverage, procedural training or formal degree structure.

audience.programmeDescription: Law at Tilburg University studies legal rules, institutions and reasoning in their social context. The Dutch-taught LLB develops private, criminal, constitutional, administrative, European and international law, practical skills and legal research, with an approved minor and a required thesis.
audience.comparisonExplanation: UCR can combine substantial legal study with politics, society, economics, ethics and empirical methods. Its options prioritise law in social context, sustainability and governance, or legal practice and organisations. Tilburg provides a more extensive Dutch doctrinal and procedural sequence; the course relationships shown are partial.
